t:
Section 2(b) of the National Housing Act is amended—

    (1) 
by striking out “$3,500” and inserting in lieu thereof “$5,000”;
 
    (2) 
by striking out “five year’s” and inserting in lieu thereof “seven years”;
 
    (3) 
by striking out “$5 discount” and inserting in lieu thereof “$5.50 discount”; and
 
    (4) 
by striking out “$1 discount” and inserting in lieu thereof “$4.50 discount”.

fable.w: This section only makes technical amendments to dollar amounts, loan terms, and discount figures in Section 2(b) of the National Housing Act. No tempting reading exists: it has no consultation, hearing, comment period, rulemaking authority, advisory body, or right to sue involving anyone outside the federal government.
fable.s: Section 2(b) of the National Housing Act is amended

qwen_block.w: This section consists entirely of technical amendments to statutory text, specifically changing monetary amounts and time periods. It does not establish any process for consultation, public comment, advisory committees, or coordination with outside parties. There is no interaction with non-federal entities described in this text.
qwen_block.s: Section 2(b) of the National Housing Act is amended— (1) by striking out “$3,500” and inserting in lieu thereof “$5,000”; (2) by striking out “five year’s” and inserting in lieu thereof “seven years”; (3) by striking out “$5 discount” and inserting in lieu thereof “$5.50 discount”; and (4) by striking out “$1 discount” and inserting in lieu thereof “$4.50 discount”.

opus.w: This section only changes numbers in Section 2(b) of the National Housing Act ($3,500 to $5,000, five years to seven years, and two discount figures). It does not require or allow rulemaking, consultation, hearings, advisory bodies, or a right to sue. Example 6 was labelled "Yes" because that amendment gave the Secretary power to act by regulation. No such power appears here, so nobody outside the federal government is brought into a federal decision.
opus.b:
1. **Analysis:** One could be tempted to read this as "Yes" because it amends the National Housing Act, and Example 6 counted a Housing Act amendment as participation. That reading fails here. In Example 6, the amendment gave the Secretary power to act "by regulation." This section only swaps out dollar amounts, a time period and discount figures. It doesn't create any rulemaking, consultation, hearing, advisory body or right to sue, and no one outside the federal government plays a part in any decision.

qwen_chat.w: This section merely amends specific monetary values and time periods in the National Housing Act. It does not create any mechanism for consultation, public comment, advisory committees, or coordination with outside parties. qwen_chat.s: Section 2(b) of the National Housing Act is amended— (1) by striking out “$3,500” and inserting in lieu thereof “$5,000”; (2) by striking out “five year’s” and inserting in lieu thereof “seven years”; (3) by striking out “$5 discount” and inserting in lieu thereof “$5.50 discount”; and (4) by striking out “$1 discount” and inserting in lieu thereof “$4.50 discount”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that changing discount amounts affects public participation in housing programs. However, the text itself only describes numerical amendments to a statute and does not establish any process for consulting with or involving outside parties in a decision.
